study.title: Luke 14 - Humility, mercy, and the cost of discipleship
study.overview: Luke 14 gathers teachings of Jesus in a context of meal in the house of a Pharisee leader. The chapter shows Jesus acting freely in the face of religious criticism, healing on the Sabbath and using the table as a place of spiritual teaching. Then he corrects the search for prestige, calls to generosity without interest, exposes the cold response of the guests to God's invitation and concludes with very serious demands for those who wish to follow him: renunciation, perseverance and discernment. The outcome with salt illustrates that a disciple without firmness loses its usefulness.

outline.title: Jesus heals on the Sabbath and exposes the hardness of observers
outline.explanation: Jesus enters a Pharisee's house to eat and finds a man with swelling in the body. In healing him on the Sabbath, he shows that mercy does not violate the will of God; on the contrary, it reveals the true meaning of the law. The silence of the Law experts and Jesus" question about saving an animal on Saturday day reveal the incoherence of a religiosity more concerned with rules than with people.

outline.title: Humility at table and generosity without interest
outline.explanation: Seeing guests competing for the best places, Jesus teaches that honor should be sought for humility, not self-examination. Then, the host advises the host to invite the poor, crippled, craze and blind, that is, people unable to repay. The true reward is not in the social exchange, but in the resurrection of the righteous.

outline.title: The parable of the great banquet and the human refusal
outline.explanation: Faced with the talk about the banquet in the Kingdom of God, Jesus narrates a supper in which the guests apologize and refuse the invitation. The lord of the house then calls the marginalized of the city and then extends the invitation to the paths and trails, until he fills his house. The picture announces that the Kingdom advances despite rejection, and that external privileges do not guarantee participation in the table of God.

outline.title: The price of discipleship and tasteless salt
outline.explanation: Jesus confronts the multitudes with the conditions of following him: to love less than Christ the strongest bonds, to carry the cross, to calculate the cost and to abandon everything that is incumbent with his landlord. Finally, tasteless salt loses its usefulness and is thrown away, warning that a disciple without perseverance and without spiritual distinction becomes unproductive.

study.context: The chapter takes place during a meal in the house of a leader of the Pharisees, on a Saturday, a scenario that Luke repeatedly uses to show Jesus teaching in public environments and at the table. The notes highlight that Jesus related to various groups at the table, including Pharisees, and took advantage of these moments to instruct, correct and reveal the Kingdom. The social context also matters: banquets were places of status, exchange of favors and prestige; therefore, Jesus' speech about places of honor, poor guests and the great banquet directly confronts the common practices of the religious and social elite.
study.theology: Luke 14 presents three central themes. First, Jesus" mercy overcomes narrow interpretations of the law: healing on the Sabbath is consistent with the divine purpose of restoring life. Second, the Kingdom of God reverses the logic of human honor: whoever exalts himself will be humiliated, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted; moreover, true generosity seeks those who cannot reward. Third, grace does not eliminate the seriousness of discipleship: following Christ involves real renunciation, absolute preference for him and willingness to carry the cross. The parable of the banquet also suggests that human refusal to God's invitation does not prevent the realization of his purpose, and that the marginalized end up being called to occupy the place of those who despised the invitation. The tasteless salt reinforces that a disciple who loses his spiritual identity ceases to fulfill his function.

scholarViews.insight: The note emphasizes that Jesus confronts the social logic of the banquets by ordering the poor and unable to repay themselves, showing that God receives sinners at his time of salvation.
Matthew Henry sees in this excerpt a lesson of humility: Jesus corrects ambition for the first places and teaches that true exaltation comes from God, not self-promotion.
Adam Clarke notes that the salt that loses the taste becomes useless and is thrown out, highlighting the total loss of utility when salt no longer retains its strength.

questions: In which areas have I sought recognition rather than serving with humility?
My way to invite, offer help, and use my resources includes people who can't give back?
Am I calculating the cost of following Jesus seriously, or treating discipleship as something secondary?
study.practice: This week, choose a concrete attitude of humility: give the place, give preference to another person or practice a generosity without expected return. Also examine whether there is any loyalty, habit or ambition that is competing with Christ. Pray that God will give you a heart willing to carry the cross, serve the excluded and remain useful as true salt in the midst of the world.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are partial in some verses and therefore the historical synthesis was limited to what they really claim. The expression "odiating" in Luke 14:26 was treated as a language of priority and renunciation in relation to Christ, without imposing a technical reading beyond the text and notes. It was also not possible to use details that did not appear clearly in the excerpts, especially about verses without explicit comment.
